newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese bank shares arouse feeding frenzy.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese bank shares arouse feeding frenzy.

text.p: After feeding for years on a rich diet of high-yield treasury bills, Lebanese investors are suddenly developing a voracious appetite for equities thanks to falling interest rates and a handful of high-flying bank shares.
The Beirut Stock Exchange witnessed a feeding frenzy this week after a third bank share, Bank of Beirut , began trading amid very heavy demand.
The three banks listed since December have transformed the once-sleepy market into a small but bustling hive of activity.

A few months ago the market traded a handful of shares daily or none at all, but this week hundreds of thousands traded each day and brokers were deluged with orders as local and Arab investors rushed to get into the game.

"I have very, very heavy demand. Today I got 46 new clients for Bank of Beirut shares alone. They want over 800,000 shares," Nabil Aoun, chairman of Fidus finance house, told Reuters on Monday, a day after BOB's April 11 debut.
Interest perked up in January after Banque Libanaise pour le Commerce and Banque Audi became the first to list under a 1996 law allowing banks to trade 30 percent of their shares.
Before that the market comprised four semi-dormant industrials and Solidere , the company rebuilding central Beirut, whose shares have been stagnant for months.
Banking has been a bright spot in the Lebanese economy since the 1975-90 civil war and the two bank shares quickly shone.
By last week BLC and Banque Audi had risen 27 percent and 30 percent respectively and when BOB shares began trading on Friday investors hurled themselves at them.
Jean Riachi, chairman of Beirut finance house Financial Funds Advisors, said money that previously went into Lebanese t-bills was now looking for new opportunities.
"The market is driven by liquidity that is beginning to flow into the stock exchange. Thank God it is only the beginning because there is not enough supply," Riachi said.
Investors signalled huge interest in bank shares in March when BOB's $10 million pre-listing private share placement was 11 times oversubscribed, attracting about $110 million.
On the first day of trading, demand for BOB was 6.5 million shares against supply of under 400,000 and the shares rose 38 percent against issue price.
After four days BOB was up 55.5 percent and BLC and Banque Audi were 33 and 34 percent above issue price.
Trading volume on the exchange, often below $1 million a day before the banks listed, rose above $3 million. Some industrial shares moved in the euphoria, though Solidere failed to budge.
Brokers and financiers were delighted by the end of a long, dull period since the Beirut Stock Exchange reopened in January 1996, but some had reservations about what it all meant.
"Yes, it's a bull run, but it's also a bottleneck situation," said Riachi. "We need more supply to make it more consistent.
"We need more companies on the stock exchange to see if it will become significant in this country. It is still too small to talk about a bright emerging market."
He and several brokers cautioned about the surge in BOB shares, saying they rose due to excess market liquidity and were now expensive and speculative.
Officials at BOB and Middle East Capital Group which managed its share placement replied that the bank had good fundamentals and the price rise was the result of supply and demand.
According to Nicholas Sawwan of Lebanon Invest, BOB is now "slightly more speculative" than other bank shares with the highest P/E ratio based on estimated 1997 earnings.
"But the street estimates for 1997 could be conservative as the bank has had a good turnaround in the past four years," he said.
Sawwan attributed the market surge to the size of the BOB issue and excess liquidity.

"What we are witnessing is the result of the BOB share placement oversubscription," he said. "There is excess liquidity from BOB. The money that came in does not want to leave Lebanon and it's looking for opportunities.
"The BOB issue is very small and it is creating frustration among investors. Maybe we are seeing inflated demand," Sawwan added.
However, the jump in all three bank shares could prove justified if first-quarter results, due this month, were good.
"We feel on the street that earnings are good. If they come in higher than expected then this price jump will be more than justified," Sawwan said.
"The time is ripe for other banks to come to the market. The euphoria is all over Lebanon. They should hurry up," he added.
